newsitem.title: USA: Soy prices up on frost, Iraq tensions lift crude.
newsitem.headline: Soy prices up on frost, Iraq tensions lift crude.

text.p: New forecasts that suggested a crop-damaging frost could soon hit the U.S. Midwest sent soybean prices sharply higher at the Chicago Board of Trade.
Crude oil prices moved above $24 per barrel in reaction heightened tensions in Iraq, while lumber prices tumbled amid weakening cash markets.
The bullish frost forecasts overpowered concerns by traders who were reluctant to enter new positions ahead of new crop production estimates Wednesday by the U.S. Agriculture Department.
"The belief is even with a bearish report we're going to be better on beans anyway because we're going to frost them to death," said Steve Bruce, analyst with E.D. and F. Man International.
Analysts expect the Agriculture Department to reduce its U.S. soybean crop estimate from its August estimate of 2.30 billion bushels.

Soybeans were planted late in the U.S. Midwest and susceptible to damage should there be a frost the next few weeks. Frost halts the ripening process of the soybeans, lowering the quality of the vegetable oil produced by the soybeans.
Below normal temperatures were expected across much of the U.S. Midwest this week as a slow-moving cold front pushes across the region, meteorologists said.

"All this warm summer weather we've seen in the Midwest is going to come crashing to a halt," said Mike Palmerino, meteorologist with Weather Services Corp. "Thursday, Friday, and into the weekend, temperatures are really going to drop off."
Although no frost was forecast this week for the Midwest soybean areas, crop experts believe it will arrive soon because meteorologists expect a long-term cold pattern for the Midwest.
CBOT soybeans for November delivery rose 13-1/4 cents to $8.07 per bushel. November reflects the price of soybeans at harvest this fall.

News Iraq was rebuilding damaged air defences, plus allegations from Baghdad, which the U.S. denied, that three missiles were fired at U.S. warplanes, prompted buying in London and New York Mercantile Exchange crude oil markets.
The actions fuelled expectations among oil traders that tensions with Iraq will escalate.
"We have warned Saddam Hussein that we retain the right and will, in fact, take actions necessary to protect our pilots," said a U.S. Pentagon spokesman.
The NYMEX October crude oil rose 39 cents to $24.12 per barrel, and analysts said the contract may soon reach the contract high of $24.25.
October gasoline closed up 0.76 cent at 64.85 cents per gallon and October heating oil was up 0.72 at 66.67 cents.
Lumber futures at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange fell for limit losses of $10.00 per thousand board feet in November and January contracts largely prompted by slowing demand for cash lumber.
November closed limit down at $374.50 per tbf.
"The cash (market) does look like its slowing down," said Curt Cunningham, president of Pacific Futures Trading.
Expectations are for cash spruce, which is deliverable against CME lumber futures to be quoted steady or possibly lower this week.
Lumber prices had strong gains in recent weeks as lumber dealers, who let inventories run low, scrambled to supply home builders.
